newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa's murder rate drops.
newsitem.headline: South Africa's murder rate drops.

text.p: South Africa's murder rate averaged 65 a day for the first three months of this year, police said on Friday, down from about 69 a day in the same period last year.
Police figures showed 5,863 murders were reported from January to March, accounting for a five percent drop over the same period last year when 6,175 cases were recorded.

"Crime levels remain intolerably high in our country (but) this is a marked improvement of the crime picture in South Africa since elections in 1994," Police Minister Sydney Mufamadi told a briefing where the statistics were released.

A total of 6,802 murders were committed in 1994. President Nelson Mandela's government has largely subdued the political killing that plagued the country then but violent crimes have soared, prompting public calls for hanging to be restored and a state of emergency introduced.
Mufamadi said his department hoped to consolidate its "modest gains" with immediate and longer-term measures, but ruled out any emotive response by the government.
"We think the situation is very serious, but it does not warrant a panic response," he said.
South Africa recently experienced a renewed wave of high-profile violent crimes, with raids on banks and foreign exchange bureaus in the limelight.

But police said their figures showed the situation was not as bleak as depicted, reporting a total of 121 bank robberies for the first three months of this year, a fall of 40 percent from 1996. Robberies of cash in transit were down a dramatic 52 percent.
The banking industry estimates that robberies cost it some $25 million a year, and some branches in high-risk areas recently threatened to close on Saturdays to protect staff.

Mufamadi said army troops would be brought in to help police safeguard banks in key areas to avert the closures. While declining to give details, he said the focus would be in the Gauteng region centred on Johannesburg.

Police said priority crimes which remained a problem were rapes, which had risen by 2.7 percent to 13,414 -- equal to 149 rapes a day. Truck hijackings rose by 4.6 percent to total 865 and car hijackings were up by 1.7 percent, totalling 3,144.

Mufamadi last month lifted a 1994 moratorium on new police recruits and allocated $33 million for hiring 5,250 civilian and uniformed officers. He called in a leading businessman to overhaul the police force, winning praise from business, politicians and the media.
